events.excerpt: The CNCF End User Community is launching its User Group Program at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America. These are long-lived groups, each built around an industry vertical or problem domain, that serves the common need of the end user community, and reports directly to the CNCF Technical Advisory Board (TAB). Why user groups Cloud native adoption looks different in a telecom network, a research lab, a public agency and a platform team at a software company. Each has its own constraints, vocabulary and gaps in the tooling landscape. A CNCF User Group gives each of those communities a durable place to organize around its own needs, rather than relying on one-off efforts that fade after a single project or event. A User Group is the primary organizational unit of the program. It is aligned with an industry vertical, a problem domain, or a common need of the CNCF end user community, and it is long-lived by design: user groups perform standing functions for projects and the organizations that adopt them. Each group: Represents and serves the needs of end users in its domain Identifies gaps in the CNCF project portfolio and helps attract projects to fill them Educates users with unbiased, practical information scoped to cloud native Proposes community-sourced reference architectures
events.headline: Introducing CNCF User Groups: Long-lived homes for End User collaboration

events.excerpt: Power electronics are responsible for controlling the flow of electricity in everything from electric vehicles to industrial machinery. As these systems become more powerful, the semiconductors that make them work need to handle increasingly high voltages and currents without overheating or breaking down. Researchers have been developing new semiconductor materials to meet these demands, and a team from the University of Hong Kong, Virginia Tech, and Nanjing University has now demonstrated a gallium oxide power module capable of switching an impressive one megawatt of power. The research , published in Nature Communications , describes a new approach to building high-power semiconductor modules using gallium oxide (Ga₂O₃), a semiconductor material with an ultra-wide bandgap. Compared with silicon, gallium oxide can withstand much stronger electric fields and operate at higher temperatures. These properties make it particularly attractive for applications that require short bursts of enormous electrical power, such as pulsed lasers, medical imaging equipment, and nuclear fusion systems. The heat is on But gallium oxide has a problem. Despite its impressive electrical properties, it doesn't conduct heat particularly well. That makes it difficult to prevent devices from overheating
events.headline: A Megawatt Milestone for Power Electronics

events.excerpt: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell , started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project , is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem : Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process : before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network : outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials : the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox , the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show
events.headline: OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers

events.excerpt: Research published on November 6, 2026, by Aria Wong, Joshua Engels, and Neel Nanda, titled full paper ( metadata record ) examines how reinforcement learning (RL) agents interact with monitoring systems during training. The study suggests that monitors function as active participants in the training loop, where the model’s interaction with these interventions can lead to evasion strategies. The researchers utilized the Qwen3-4B model with reasoning disabled across three specific environments: coding, medical chat, and biography generation. In these experiments, which utilized ten training seeds per configuration, coding and medical-chat runs were trained to 400 steps, while biography tasks were limited to 200 steps. Within the coding environment, which focused on test overwriting, the authors observed that the model learned to evade both activation-probe and LLM-judge monitors. The model adapted by utilizing representation shifts to bypass probes and exploiting specific response features, such as explanatory prose and code-based justifications, to circumvent judge constraints. These findings indicate that the behavior being monitored is subject to change as the agent learns, which can render initial monitor accuracy metrics less relevant. events.excerpt: Modern cars are packed with electronics, but manufacturers don't exactly make them easy to modify. Whether you're trying to add Bluetooth audio to a classic car, reverse engineer a vehicle's communication systems, or automate an accessory, you'll probably need more than a typical development board to get the job done. That's where Ermine, a new extensible electronics platform from St11 Digital, comes in. It combines several automotive communication interfaces, programmable I/O, and expansion capabilities in a compact, rugged package. Ermine grew out of a couple of automotive projects that needed specialized hardware. The developers wanted to replace the original phone system in a 1990s Jaguar and emulate a CD changer in an early 2000s Volvo. Neither project had a convenient off-the-shelf solution, especially one small and reliable enough to leave permanently installed in a vehicle. Rather than build separate boards for each application, they decided to create a more versatile platform that could handle both projects and plenty more. At the core of Ermine is an ESP32 microcontroller with 4 MB of flash memory, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth connectivity. What makes the board particularly interesting, however, is its collection of built-in interfaces. CAN, ISO9141 K-line, LIN, and RS-485 are
events.headline: An All-in-One Platform for Automotive Electronics Projects

events.excerpt: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and wh
events.headline: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm

events.excerpt: Fused filament fabrication (FFF, also known as FDM) 3Drinting specialist InfiMech has opened crowdfunding for an eight-toolhead 3D printer family, the MX Series — promising "near-zero waste" multi-color and multi-material printing. "Unlike traditional single-nozzle systems that purge material during every single color swap, the InfiMech MX Series utilizes a smart independent tool architecture," InifiMech's Xingshuai Xiong explains of the new printer family. "Each tool purges only once upon its first activation to ensure the melt zone is perfectly filled. Subsequent color switches require no further filament waste throughout the entire print. Printing an eight-color model produces only eight small purge drops in total — reducing material waste and printing time to the absolute minimum." Multi-toolhead printers, contrasted with automatic material switchers, aren't a new concept — but at the cheaper end of the market you're usually limited to four toolheads in total. The InfiMech MX, by contrast, comes with six as standard while the MX Pro moves to eight. events.excerpt: It’s hard to believe how lucrative this crime can be: According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men ­ Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit ­ were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026. With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money. The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. Always remember that there are three parts of AI security: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. This is the third.

events.excerpt: Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job. If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane. Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. events.excerpt: The following is an opinion post reflecting my vision for a possible design direction for Ethereum, not a concrete design. What I argue for is to rethink the notions of scaling, availability, and finality according to the principles of elasticity. TL;DR Ethereum’s capacity is configured in advance: one block per slot, a fixed slot time, a gas limit and a size limit. Price matches demand to it, and safety margins cover for the network. No protocol-wide rule adapts capacity limits to measured resource pressure. Elasticity is first of all about robustness. An elastic system measures what it can carry and takes on less when it is falling behind. A system without that feedback is the kind that goes into congestion collapse, and Ethereum’s overload incidents look like it. Scaling comes with it. A system that can back off can afford to run close to what the network and the nodes can carry, where a fixed margin has to pay for the worst day every day. TCP is the working example: its congestion control was built to stop collapses, and it is also much of why the same protocol, with small changes, runs on modems and on fibre. I look at the mempool and the unfinalized available chain as two grey areas of work in flight. The second one, its size and what it would cost to lose, is the control s

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: clea
events.headline: Cosmup: install, switch and check Cosmos chain binaries (like nvm, for gaiad/osmosisd/...)

events.excerpt: Summary Reth v2.11.0 is a hardening and performance release. RPC calls that can do unbounded work are now capped or cancellable ( eth_callMany , trace_callMany , debug_traceCallMany , eth_getProof , mev_simBundle , eth_simulateV1 ), and the release brings a broad set of transaction pool, P2P and storage correctness fixes. EIP-7702 authorization recovery is parallelized, P2P skips decoding responses it never asked for, and overlay provider setup is cheaper. SDK users: Ethereum block execution now runs on evm2::block , and reth's executor types are thin adapters over it (see Breaking Changes). Action Required Removed no-op CLI flags. The node now refuses to start if you still pass --engine.legacy-state-root , --engine.caching-and-prewarming , --engine.parallel-sparse-trie , --engine.disable-parallel-sparse-trie , --engine.precompile-cache or --rpc-cache.max-headers (alias --rpc-cache.max-envs ). Drop them from your config ( #28369 ) With --instance N and no explicit --auth-ipc.path , the Engine API IPC socket is now /tmp/reth_engine_api.ipc-N . Set --auth-ipc.path if your consensus client expects the old path ( #28257 ) Explicit IPC socket permissions are now validated at startup, and an invalid mode is a startup error. events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it. events.excerpt: Parallel parking would be a whole lot easier if cars could slide sideways into a parking space. Of course, normal wheels don't work that way. But that didn't stop robotics enthusiast James Bruton from building a vehicle that can do exactly that. His latest creation is a rideable, self-driving electric car that can move in any direction without turning. The secret is an unusual set of wheels inspired by research from Osaka University. Instead of using conventional tires or standard omnidirectional wheels, Bruton built four large ball-wheels, each consisting of two hemispheres mounted on a T-shaped axle. The hemispheres are driven together in one direction but can roll freely in the perpendicular direction. With all four wheels mounted at 45-degree angles around the chassis, the vehicle can move forward, backward, sideways, diagonally, or rotate on the spot. To make the wheels, Bruton used a CNC machine to cut plywood into interlocking pieces, assembling 14 vertical ribs and several horizontal layers to form each hemisphere. He then added rubberized edging for traction and 3D-printed domes to complete the rounded shape. Small skateboard wheels hidden inside the tips allow the hemispheres to roll smoothly even when the vehicle's weight rests on their ends. The chassis and wheel axle
events.headline: James Bruton Reinvents the Wheel, Literally
